answer.evidence: The stairs are four repeating steps. Each step has a light 1-row edge line (rows 0, 8, 16, 24), then about 4-5 rows of lighter stone tread, then 2-3 rows of dark riser shadow (rows 6-7, 13-15, 21-23, 29-31). This gives horizontal tread bands with front edges and shadows. A textured cliff face of 16 rows (32-47) sits below as the south vertical face. The side strips of grass and dirt at the left and right edges are flat terrain, not an isometric side face.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a small stair piece with wooden posts at the sides and horizontal stone treads. Measured facts: 6 visible tones per tile (reference grass 3, paving 7), 0% near-flat coverage, and 24% neutral dark edge pixels, so outlines are mostly tinted. Each tread is a light grey band with a dark grey underside and a few speckles. That gives about 3 steps per material against roughly 5-6 in the paving reference, whose stones are shaded one by one with distinct highlights, mids and shadows. The wooden posts are thin and nearly flat (about 2-3 browns). The treads read as repeated, uniform stripes with little per-stone variation. The tile density is therefore a bit below the paving reference, though it is not flat or sticker-like. The piece is not clearly at reference quality for shading depth and texture, so it fails.

The whole piece uses only 14 distinct colours, against 80 in the grass reference, and the paving reference has more stone-by-stone variation and edge highlights. It looks a little thinner and more schematic than a Beodeul piece, and when in doubt this fails.
